newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: DEA chief announces crackdown on Colombian heroin.
newsitem.headline: DEA chief announces crackdown on Colombian heroin.

text.p: The head of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration said on Tuesday that Washington and Bogota would together create a force to try to stem the growing flow of Colombian heroin into the United States.

The specialist anti-heroin unit, to be based in Bogota, will be made up of DEA agents and their Colombian National Police counterparts. The two countries will pool intelligence efforts and funds and share logistical support.

During a seven-hour visit to Bogota, the DEA chief, Thomas Constantine, said a new breed of Colombian heroin traffickers had emerged, independent of the once powerful cocaine mobs, and were now supplying almost two-thirds of the heroin seized on U.S. streets.

"About 63 percent of all heroin we seize in the United States comes from Colombia. That doesn't mean to say 63 percent of all the heroin entering the United States is from Colombia, but it's a pretty good indication," Constantine told foreign reporters just before ending his lightning visit.
He said the biggest market for heroin was on the East Coast of the United States, where as much as 90 percent came from Colombia and was distributed by dealers originally from the Dominican Republic.

The hardest-hit cities, Constantine said, were Baltimore; Boston; Orlando, Florida; and New York. He added that Mexican "black tar" heroin continued to dominate the West Coast market. The market share of Southeast Asian heroin and that from Pakistan and Afghanistan has dropped sharply, he said.
Colombian heroin is up to 90 percent pure and sells wholesale for about $85,000 per 2.2 pounds (1 kg) and for as much as $270,000 retail on the streets, Constantine said.
The DEA boss held talks with National Police chief Gen. Rosso Jose Serrano and Col. Leonel Gallego, both of whom have headed the fight against Colombia's notorious drug mobs.
He praised the skill of Colombian police in anti-narcotics operations, describing them as "one of the most professional forces in the hemisphere."

A joint statement by Constantine and Serrano announcing the creation of the new anti-heroin unit said, "The creation of a Special Bi-national Group against heroin trafficking ... is an association to intensify our efforts to control the production, the trade and the organisations that traffic heroin."

Constantine did not meet with President Ernesto Samper, whom U.S. officials insist is a "truly corrupt president" in light of allegations that he accepted $6 million in drug money to finance his 1994 presidential campaign.

But in comments to the local media, Samper said Constantine's words of praise for this Andean nation's anti-drug fight were a "breath of fresh air." U.S.-Colombian relations sank to an all-time low last March when Washington blacklisted Colombia for the second consecutive year for its failure to crack down hard enough on drug trafficking.

That decision did not affect counternarcotics aid. In 1997 the United States gave about $80 million in anti-drug aid to Colombia, together with a multimillion-dollar package of crop-dusters, helicopters and fast riverboats.

Last week the State Department released about $70 million in additional aid to the Colombian military to be used in combating drugs. Both the Colombian army and police play a lead counternarcotics role.

Unlike the Colombian authorities, Constantine downplayed the links between the country's leftist guerrillas and the drug trade. He conceded that guerrillas might work for drug cartels but rejected suggestions that they were taking the lion's share of the illicit profits.
